title: Argon2id kernel compiled for sm_75 (Tesla T4): SASS and a block-copy A/B
how: Kaggle notebook on a Tesla T4 (40 SMs, 14.6 GiB, CUDA 13.0.88), built and run by src/sass/kaggle_t4_argon2id.py. The device source is sliced straight out of src/cuda/cuda_argon2.cu, so the shipped variant really is the shipped code; only fill_block is swapped.

measured.params: m=19456 KiB, t=2, p=1 (the real Anubis parameters)
measured.shape: 64 concurrent hashes (1.19 GiB resident) x 8 reps
measured.correctness: both variants produce the identical 32-byte tag, checked before timing

compiler_report.note: 255 registers is the T4 maximum: the kernel is at the register wall and already spills 6 bytes. The 416-byte stack frame is inherited from H0/H' and the 16-word schedules, not from this change.

what_changed: block copy moved from 8-byte scalars to 16-byte uint4: 64 threads cover a 1 KiB block in one iteration instead of two, and a warp request is 512 B instead of 256 B

prev^ref is saved in a second shared array (sP), so the final xor does not re-read prev and ref from memory. The shipped form reads 2 KiB, then re-reads the same 2 KiB; on a random-access workload that second read is pure L2 traffic, and it is now gone
the permutation is byte-identical in both variants - it is the algorithm, and it was already cooperative (one block per CUDA block, 64 threads, shared sR)
what_was_not_changed_and_why: only 32 of the 64 threads do G work in each half-phase (the gi < 4 guard), and the two halves are separated by a barrier because G4..G7 read words G0..G3 wrote. Fixing that means 32 threads holding 4 words each in registers with __shfl-based lanes - the classic warp-cooperative Argon2 kernel - which is a full rewrite of fill_block, not a copy-path change

the 255-register wall and 6 bytes of spill: H0/H' with 16-word schedules and the BLAKE2b compression dominate register pressure. Shrinking it would raise occupancy, which matters because this kernel is memory-latency bound
where_the_time_goes: 38,912 blocks per hash x 3 KiB of random traffic is 139 MB per hash; at 715 H/s that is ~102 GB/s of random 1 KiB accesses on a 320 GB/s part, so the block copy is the right thing to attack first. The 1.34x says the copy was costing about a quarter of the run.
next_if_anyone_wants_it: the warp-cooperative fill_block (32 threads, block in registers, __syncwarp instead of __syncthreads) is the remaining big lever; it is an algorithm-level rewrite of the same function that was just measured to matter
